title: The end date is not the goal date
objectives: Explain what happens when a SIP's registered tenure ends.
Use the renewal illustration to show why renewing beats simply holding.
body_md:
When a SIP's registered tenure ends, only the instalments stop. The units already bought stay invested and keep moving with the market until the investor redeems them. That is why the end date is not the goal date.

## The arithmetic of forgetting

₹10,000 a month for ten years, at an assumed 12% a year, grows to about ₹23.2 lakh.

- Stop and simply hold for ten more years: about ₹72.2 lakh at year 20.
- Renew the SIP for those ten years: about ₹99.9 lakh at year 20.

The existing units compound either way. Renewing adds the extra years of contributions. Many investors simply forget to renew, so put the end date in the client's review calendar and call three months before it.

## What to say when the end date arrives

- Confirm the goal date and the target amount first; the answer decides everything.
- If the goal is years away, renew with a step-up rather than a flat renewal.
- If the goal is near, start the glide path instead of renewing into equity.
- Write the new end date down, for the client and for your calendar.
example: Anil's 10-year SIP ended last month and his child's college fund is needed in 8 years. His units are worth about ₹23.2 lakh. Renewing with a step-up for those eight years adds contributions while the existing corpus keeps compounding.
say: Your SIP's end date stops the instalments, not the investment.
With eight years to the goal, renewing and stepping up adds the years that matter.
never: The SIP has ended, so the money is now safe.
The fund house will automatically renew it for you.
